tldr: By combining explicit rhythm generation from a central pattern generator (CPG) with a neural network that maps leg trajectories to joint angles, this paper achieves five distinct gaits and seamless transitions between them using a single reinforcement learning policy with high success rates.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed CPG–ENN method. An eight-neuron CPG generates gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) translates rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters into joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. The reinforcement learning policy modulates only six physically interpretable trajectory variables via feedback.
overview:
Just like a newborn foal can stand and walk almost immediately, animal locomotion relies on an innate rhythmic neural mechanism. At the same time, experience and training refine those movements, as seen in a well-trained horse performing precise steps. In legged robot control, combining this innate rhythm generation (via central pattern generators, or CPGs) with learned motor adaptation has long been an open challenge.

Traditional CPG-based approaches often require manual parameter tuning for each gait, struggle to accurately track target velocities, and frequently suffer from velocity drops or falls during gait transitions. Conversely, recent reinforcement learning (RL) methods often demand separate policies per gait or intricately hand-crafted rewards dedicated solely to gait transitions.

To address this, the authors propose CPG–ENN, a framework that cleanly decouples explicit rhythm generation from learned motion execution. An eight-neuron CPG produces the rhythmic coordination, while a leg-shared execution neural network (ENN), pretrained offline with inverse kinematics (IK), outputs joint-angle references. The reinforcement learning policy only needs to adjust six physically intuitive trajectory parameters, such as stride length and base height.

Through simulation and real-robot experiments on a Unitree Go2, a single policy successfully controls five distinct gaits—walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk. It achieves an outstanding 99.39% transition success rate across all 20 directed gait pairs. Remarkably, the authors discovered that even without explicit exposure to transitions during training, basic transition feasibility remains near 100%. Transition training primarily serves to polish the smoothness and speed recovery during gait switches.
contributions: Proposed a clean control architecture that decouples rhythm generation (CPG) from joint-space motion realization (a pretrained, leg-shared ENN), modulating only six physically interpretable trajectory variables.
Achieved five distinct gaits and smooth cross-gait transitions using a single reinforcement learning policy, without gait-specific learned controllers or transition-specific reward engineering.
Conducted an exhaustive evaluation of cross-gait transitions across all 20 directed gait pairs and multiple speed regimes, demonstrating a high transition success rate of 99.39%.

Revealed through ablation studies that transition training is not strictly necessary for transition feasibility itself; instead, exposure mainly refines transient responses by reducing velocity error and convergence time.

sections.heading: Refining Innate Biological Rhythms Through Learning
sections.summary: Inspired by how animals combine innate rhythms with learned adaptation, this work proposes CPG–ENN, uniting explicit CPG rhythm generation with neural motion execution. It aims to achieve five gaits, precise velocity tracking, and highly reliable transitions under a single policy.
sections.details:
Animals can walk shortly after birth, but experience subsequently refines their limb coordination. Locomotion is inherently a hybrid of structurally organized innate rhythms and flexible learned behaviors. In robotics, adopting this perspective offers an attractive architecture where explicit rhythmic coordination is preserved while reinforcement learning provides environmental adaptability.

Prior CPG methods demonstrated multi-gait transitions across five gaits, but scaling stride parameters alone struggled to precisely match target velocities, often causing significant velocity fluctuations or failures during transitions. Alternatively, methods that solve inverse kinematics (IK) online to generate trajectories suffer from high computational overhead and kinematic singularities.

This is the starting point of the paper. The authors preserve the explicit coordination of a CPG while offloading the foot-trajectory-to-joint-angle mapping to a neural network (ENN: Execution Neural Network) pretrained offline. As a result, a single reinforcement learning feedback policy needs to modulate only six intuitive parameters. This controller reliably governs five gaits (walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk) on a physical Unitree Go2 robot and switches between them with a near-100% success rate.

captions.F1: Snapshots of the five gaits (walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk) deployed on the physical Unitree Go2. Dynamic jumping gaits are clearly demonstrated, including highlighted flight phases and clearance (4.1 cm for bound, 5 cm for pronk).

sections.heading: How Have CPGs and Reinforcement Learning Evolved Together?
sections.summary: The authors review prior work combining CPGs with reinforcement learning, as well as methods managing multiple gaits and their transitions. The proposed approach is unique: rather than modifying internal oscillator states, it delegates joint-space conversion to a shared network pretrained on explicit foot trajectories.
sections.details:
### II-A Learning-Based and CPG-Based Legged Locomotion
In hybrid controllers combining CPGs and reinforcement learning (RL), a core design difference lies in where learned feedback enters the control pipeline. For instance, PMTG (Policies Modulating Trajectory Generators) modulates trajectory generator parameters while adding residual output offsets. CPG-RL directly alters oscillator amplitude and frequency, while other studies feed driving inputs into CPG dynamics like descending cortical signals. Other approaches optimize differentiable CPGs and perceptual MLPs end-to-end. In contrast, the method in this paper decouples joint-angle realization as a static, pretrained mapping that takes CPG rhythms and foot trajectory parameters as inputs.

### II-B Multi-Gait Locomotion and Gait Transitions
Prior multi-gait approaches include Mixture of Experts architectures, phase-guided controllers that supply explicit leg phase, and methods that produce natural gait transitions via energy minimization. Notably, Walk These Ways (WTW) exposed gait and posture parameters for diverse behaviors, and AllGaits achieved nine distinct gaits by combining coupled oscillators with online IK. Unlike these systems, the proposed framework completely avoids online IK. Instead, an independently defined Cartesian foot trajectory serves as training data for a leg-shared ENN that instantaneously generates joint-angle targets.

sections.heading: A Clean Separation: Explicit Rhythms and Learned Joint Mapping
sections.summary: This section details the CPG–ENN architecture. The CPG supplies gait-specific phase differences, and an ENN trained on independent foot trajectories outputs joint references. The RL policy uses a Beta distribution to modulate six bounded trajectory variables across a two-stage curriculum.
sections.details:
### III-A Overview
The system comprises three primary components: an eight-neuron CPG governing rhythm, an ENN generating joint-angle targets, and an Actor (reinforcement learning policy) that adjusts ENN inputs based on sensory feedback. Here, "trainable" does not mean optimizing the CPG dynamics themselves; rather, it refers to learning the motion realization (ENN) and the feedback modulation (Actor). Once pretrained, the ENN weights remain frozen.

### III-B Locomotion Prior via CPG–ENN
- **CPG Rhythm Generation**: Based on the Stein model, eight neurons are configured into a thigh layer (4 neurons) and a shank layer (4 neurons). Adjusting intra-layer and inter-layer synaptic weights produces the characteristic phase differences for the five gaits. States are integrated using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method.
- **Trajectory Parameterization**: Cartesian foot trajectories are independently defined using six variables: base height $h$, duty factor $d$, ground clearance $g_c$, ground penetration $g_p$, stride length $l_s$, and heading angle $\psi$, then mapped to joint angles via offline IK.
- **Learned Joint Realization (ENN)**: A single MLP shared across all four legs. Its inputs include per-leg CPG states and derivatives (4D), a one-hot gait vector (5D), leg indicators for front/hind and left/right (2D), and the six normalized trajectory parameters. On the test set, it achieves high precision with a mean absolute error (MAE) in foot position of only $1.09\,\mathrm{mm}$.

### III-C Reinforcement Learning for Trajectory Modulation
- **Observation and Action Spaces**: The Critic receives privileged information including linear velocity in the robot frame, while the Actor observes a 66-dimensional partial observation excluding it. The Actor outputs a 6-dimensional action ($h_t, g_{c,t}, g_{p,t}, l_{s,t}, \delta_t^{\mathrm{turn}}, \psi_t$), where turning is realized by establishing an asymmetric stride difference between the left and right sides.
- **Reward Function**: Consists only of four task rewards (such as velocity tracking and normalized command tracking) and nine regularization terms penalizing high energy, joint limits, and foot slippage. Because the CPG enforces rhythmic coordination, no rewards are needed to mandate foot contact timing or stylistic gait constraints.
- **Bounded Actions via Beta Policy**: Physical parameters naturally possess strict bounds. Clipping standard Gaussian samples creates discrepancies between sampled and executed actions, destabilizing training. To prevent this, the policy employs independent Beta distributions that natively match finite action intervals.

### III-D Training Procedure
Stage 1 employs a four-phase curriculum starting from trot and progressively expanding coverage to all five gaits. Stage 2 replaces 50% of episodes with 20 directed cross-gait transitions. During transitions, all gait CPGs share a common absolute time (Common-Time), allowing immediate state handover at the current time without oscillator resets or phase blending.

captions.F2: Detailed signal flow of the CPG–ENN framework. High-level commands and observations guide the Actor to output trajectory modulations. These, along with CPG neural states, feed into the leg-shared ENN to produce joint commands $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{des}}_t$ for the PD controller.

sections.heading: Five Gaits, Arbitrary Transitions, and Hardware Validation
sections.summary: The authors report multi-directional velocity tracking, 20 cross-gait transitions, comparisons against AllGaits and WTW, and physical Go2 deployments. CPG–ENN attains a 99.39% transition success rate, and ablations reveal that transition training is not strictly required for feasible switching.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Simulations ran in Isaac Gym across 4,096 parallel environments on an RTX 3090 GPU. The policy and CPG–ENN control loop operates at $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$, while physics simulation and PD control run at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$. On the physical Unitree Go2, the model runs zero-shot on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson NX without additional fine-tuning, streaming joint targets at $500\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

### IV-B Single-Policy Multi-Gait Locomotion
Across random command changes every 5 seconds in forward velocity $v_x^b$, lateral velocity $v_y^b$, and yaw rate $\omega_z^b$, all five gaits tracked commands accurately. Forward velocity RMSE stayed within $0.073$ to $0.149\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and yaw rate RMSE remained between $0.052$ and $0.098\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Visualizing the policy actions showed physically intuitive strategies: increasing stride length for higher speeds, tilting foot trajectory heading $\psi_t$ for lateral commands, and creating bilateral stride differences for turning.

### IV-C Unified Multi-Gait Transitions
Continuous sequence experiments evaluated transitions: walk $\to$ trot $\to$ pace $\to$ bound $\to$ pronk, as well as the reverse sequence. Although minor velocity dips occurred immediately after switches, speeds recovered rapidly. Forward velocity RMSE was bounded between $0.0402$ and $0.0764\,\mathrm{m/s}$, with peak average roll and pitch deviations remaining minimal at $0.0434\,\mathrm{rad}$ and $0.0726\,\mathrm{rad}$.

### IV-D Comparative Evaluation Across Gait–Speed Space
CPG–ENN was compared against AllGaits and Walk These Ways (WTW).
- **Constant Speed Tracking**: Across commands from $0.3$ to $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, CPG–ENN never fell, maintaining an average error below $0.10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in the training range ($0.3$ to $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$). In bound and pronk, it tracked out-of-distribution speeds up to $2.34\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $2.98\,\mathrm{m/s}$. In contrast, AllGaits halted at higher speeds, and WTW suffered from low bound reliability and poor pronk accuracy.
- **Gait–Speed Transition Grid**: Across an exhaustive grid of 20 gait pairs $\times$ 16 speed pairs $\times$ 21 switch timings, CPG–ENN achieved a **99.39%** success rate (versus $91.41\%$ for AllGaits and $95.63\%$ for WTW). Furthermore, its velocity RMSE on successful runs was $0.133\,\mathrm{m/s}$, roughly half that of the baselines.

### IV-E Ablation Studies: Why Do Transitions Succeed?
Here lies the most intriguing finding: a policy trained completely without Stage 2 (no transition episodes) still achieved a **99.5%** transition success rate. This indicates that the core framework—coupling explicit CPGs, a shared ENN, and bounded parameter modulation—naturally endows the system with transition capability. Stage 2 transition training did not make transitions possible; rather, it refined transient behavior, reducing target gait acquisition time from $0.772\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.714\,\mathrm{s}$ and decreasing velocity integral absolute error (IAE) by $12.6\%$.
Additionally, while naive Gaussian clipping caused a sharp drop in success, both Beta policies and tanh-squashed Gaussians maintained 100% success, confirming the critical role of properly enforcing bounded action spaces.

sections.heading: Was Transition Training Ever Really Necessary?
sections.summary: The authors summarize the effectiveness of separating explicit CPG rhythms from learned motion realization. The revelation that transition feasibility does not require explicit transition training translates a biological insight into an engineering breakthrough, pointing toward future terrain-adaptive locomotion.
sections.details:
The proposed CPG–ENN framework successfully merges explicit neural rhythm generation with learned motor realization. Zero-shot transfer from simulation to a physical Unitree Go2 succeeded without hardware fine-tuning, outperforming existing multi-gait controllers in both transition reliability and tracking precision.

Importantly, the finding that explicit rhythm coordination and a shared motion interface inherently provide robust transition feasibility—even without explicit exposure during training—offers valuable guidance for future legged controller designs. The role of transition learning is not to make transitions possible, but to polish and refine them.

Future research directions include incorporating sensory feedback from vision and foot-contact sensing for rugged terrain, as well as developing autonomous high-level gait selection mechanisms for varying environments.

takeaways: Decoupling CPG rhythm generation from Cartesian-to-joint mapping (via the ENN) eliminates online inverse kinematics while providing a physically interpretable 6D modulation space.

Cross-gait transition feasibility is inherently supported by proper rhythmic coordination and a shared interface; reinforcement learning transition training primarily refines transient speed dips and shortens convergence time.

When applying reinforcement learning to bounded physical parameters (like stride length and base height), using strict bound-preserving distributions like Beta policies or tanh squashing is essential to prevent policy degradation.
limitations: Experiments are restricted to flat indoor surfaces, and terrain-adaptive feedback for obstacles or rough ground has not yet been integrated.
The framework lacks an autonomous high-level gait selection mechanism based on speed or terrain; gait switches currently rely on explicit external user commands.
Duty factors (contact duration ratios) are preset as fixed constants for each gait and are not dynamically modulated by the policy.
